hero.headline: DeSantis targets Medicaid fraud in Southeast Florida with new state enforcement measures
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis announced comprehensive new Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday afternoon in West Palm Beach, targeting what state officials describe as sophisticated criminal operations that have drained millions of dollars from Florida's healthcare program. The governor said the state is partnering with the Trump administration and federal agencies to combat fraud that is particularly concentrated in southeast Florida, especially in Palm Beach, Miami-Dade, and Broward counties. "Southeast Florida is one of those fraud hotspots in the United States," DeSantis said, noting that while other regions may experience worse problems, all three counties remain vulnerable to organized theft from the Medicaid system.

Shevaun L. Harris, secretary of the Agency for Healthcare Administration, detailed how investigators uncovered more than a dozen fake Medicaid providers operating in West Palm Beach. These entities, created solely to steal from the state program, were discovered through shared addresses across multiple unrelated businesses, suspicious ownership structures, and a complete absence of actual patient care. Harris characterized the problem bluntly: "This is not a paperwork issue or breakdown in process. This is fraud, plain and simple." She added a direct warning to potential fraudsters: "We have more tools, more investigators, and more resolve than ever. Find another state, because our state is closed to fraud."

The state rolled out three major initiatives to address the problem. First, AHCA is launching a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company that uses technology to identify stolen and synthetic identities and hidden ownership structures before criminals can exploit the system. The technology processes data at speeds that traditional tools cannot match, flagging suspicious activity within minutes rather than days. Second, the state has imposed enrollment freezes on high-risk provider categories, including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers. DeSantis criticized the previous approach of paying fraudulent claims first and investigating them years later. Third, AHCA is requiring all active Medicaid providers to revalidate their credentials and identity, with removal from the program for those who fail to respond.

Harris reported that Florida's fraud prevention efforts have already recovered and prevented 136.45 million dollars in fraudulent spending. In the past two years alone, AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers. DeSantis credited Dr. Mehmet Oz at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for supporting the initiative, while the state also coordinated with Attorney General James Uthmeier's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit through enhanced information sharing. Florida's Medicaid program serves nearly 4 million recipients statewide. The announcement reflects DeSantis's emphasis on fiscal responsibility, as Florida has achieved four consecutive years of state budget reductions while maintaining essential services.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after Thursday night shooting leaves another teen critically injured
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old faces an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One suspect was caught by a sheriff's office K9, and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene.

The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice. Fort Pierce police have not released the names of either the suspect or victim because both are juveniles.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murdering 76-year-old grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, now faces murder charges in the February death of Patricia Ann DiBella, who was found dead at her residence on Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, faces murder and tampering with physical evidence charges in the death of his grandmother, Patricia Ann DiBella, 76. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the formal charges on Friday, June 3. DiBella was found dead inside her home at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach in February. According to investigators, Ivey admitted to killing his grandmother, who had welcomed him into her residence.

The discovery of DiBella's body came after family members requested a welfare check the day following her death. When deputies arrived at the scene, they took Ivey into custody. Since February, Ivey has remained in custody on other related charges while the investigation continued. He is now being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond as the formal murder charges move forward.

Sheriff Eric Flowers expressed the gravity of the case in a statement, saying "No one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home." Flowers also noted that he is proud of the work the investigations team did to bring justice to Patricia DiBella and her family. The sheriff encouraged anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement immediately.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office used the case to remind the community that domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone regardless of their circumstances. They provided resources for anyone in danger, including calling 911 for immediate assistance. Additional support is available through SafeSpace at 772-288-7023 or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. These services are available to anyone experiencing abuse or who knows someone in danger.

cards.headline: Curaçao national soccer team trains at FAU in Boca Raton ahead of World Cup debut
cards.teaser: Hundreds of fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium Thursday to watch Curaçao's soccer team train before the island nation makes its first-ever World Cup appearance this weekend.
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday, jerseys and flags in hand, to witness history as Curaçao prepares to make its first-ever World Cup appearance this weekend. The team, known as the "Blue Wave," held a training session that drew enthusiastic supporters eager to catch a glimpse of their favorite players ahead of the historic debut. Goalkeeper Eloy Room told WPTV that the outpouring of support has fueled the team's excitement. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today, it gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said.

Curaçao, an island nation with a population of just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches. Midfielder Tahitch Chong told WPTV the moment carries enormous meaning not just for the players, but for the entire island. Some Curaçao natives made the drive from as far as Port St. Lucie to attend the training event. Marionella Barzeycoggins, who is originally from Curaçao, said she made sure her whole family was there. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County deputy accused woman of holding phone in hand she doesn't have during traffic stop
cards.teaser: A deputy pulled over Lake Worth woman Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, but Thomas was born without a right hand.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth woman Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. Thomas was born without a right hand. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas, "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone. I mean, I saw you." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. The deputy continued pressing, asking multiple times if she had her phone in her hand. Each time, Thomas replied, "Hand to God." The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media.

Thomas has spent her life as an adaptive athlete raising awareness for the limb-difference community. The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas said she harbors no ill will toward the sheriff's office and hopes the attention helps people understand the limb-difference community. She has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. Thomas said she has no plans to sue.

hero.headline: Indian River County rental rates reach $1,222 for one-bedroom apartments, new HUD data shows
hero.teaser: Indian River County one-bedroom apartments are renting for $1,222 according to new Fair Market Rent data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, part of a regional study showing wide rental price variation across South Florida counties.
hero.body:
New data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development reveals significant rental cost variations across South Florida counties. Indian River County's Fair Market Rent for one-bedroom apartments stands at $1,222, positioning it in the mid-range of regional rates. Comparable figures for nearby areas include Okeechobee County at $1,032 and St. Lucie and Martin areas at $1,467. These figures demonstrate the substantial pricing differences that exist even within the same region of Florida.

Real estate broker Talbot Sutter, president of Sutter and Nugent Real Estate, attributes rental price variations to specific market factors. "A lot of it has to do with school districts, especially Wellington. They have like top A-rated schools, lifestyle — they have so many aspects from equestrian to outdoor activities," Sutter said. Location advantages and available amenities directly influence what landlords can charge and what renters must pay. Sutter works primarily with high-end clients, often executives relocating from New York City, who lease luxury properties before making permanent purchase decisions. He notes that demand for properties with more acreage and land has increased across the rental market.

HUD's Fair Market Rent data serves as a tool for understanding current market conditions across different areas. The agency calculates these figures using surveys, rental listings and market adjustments to reflect rates for similar properties in each region. However, these numbers do not function as rent control limits or restrict what landlords can charge tenants. Rather, they help government agencies calculate housing assistance program benefits and provide market reference points. The broader South Florida rental market continues reflecting significant affordability challenges as residents attempt to balance income growth against rapidly climbing living costs.

For renters seeking to navigate these competitive markets, Sutter recommends conducting thorough research before committing to a lease. "Know the market, do your comps. You have to really, really know the area if you don't want to get ripped off paying rent," Sutter said. Understanding comparable rental prices in specific neighborhoods and ZIP codes can help potential tenants identify fair rates and avoid overpaying. This data provides essential information for renters, policymakers and housing advocates working to address the regional affordability gaps that continue affecting South Florida communities.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast moves cats to thrift stores during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two Stuart thrift stores to house adoptable cats while its Palm City shelter undergoes major renovations to adoption, customer service, and intake areas.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is temporarily housing adoptable cats at its two thrift stores while undergoing major renovations at its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, shifting many cats to the store locations due to unavailable shelter cages. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," spokesperson Sarah Fisher said Thursday. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside merchandise for sale at both locations.

The organization is seeking temporary foster homes for other animals during the ongoing construction. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted, adding that donations of gently used goods are welcome. The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st Street in Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Hundreds of fish found dead in Port St. Lucie community after city algae treatment
cards.teaser: Hundreds of dead fish floated on the water at the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St.
cards.body:
Dead fish floated on the water at the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday following an algae treatment earlier in the week. Neighbors shared videos with WPTV showing dead fish in their backyards Thursday morning. The city hired SOLitude on Tuesday and Wednesday to treat the water for algae. Experts told WPTV that high heat combined with algae treatment can make water uninhabitable for aquatic life. Jim Herbert, a resident, described the scene: "There were hundreds and hundreds of fish here, and thousands of those little ones just gulping the air." Jerry Cook, another neighbor, expressed skepticism about quick fixes: "I don't think this is an overnight fix. I don't think it's a couple months fix. I think it's a few years fix." Herbert noted this is at least the second fish die-off since he moved to the neighborhood.

On Thursday, city crews removed dead fish and tested oxygen levels in the water. Scott Samples with the city of Port St. Lucie said officials have been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions. "We're hoping that there might be a couple of options soon," Samples said. "But those are sort of dependent on a couple of things, and so we have not been able to do that yet." Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, recommended natural solutions including planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that fuels algae growth. "We're going to end up in a cycle that we can't break unless we go back to square one and start with a natural remediation," Moir said.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce marks 25th anniversary with rare live displays
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce houses more species than many larger facilities in fully live ecosystem models dating back to 1980 under the Smithsonian.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce showcases Florida's coastal habitats through fully live, complex ecosystem displays. Manager Bill Hoffman said the facility's philosophy of presenting live models sets it apart from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said. The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a large tank recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, including a four-inch barracuda housed in the displays.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance. "You'll likely touch animals you've never seen before," said Chelsie Corcoran, exhibit educator. The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station and aims to raise public awareness about ocean threats while inspiring conservation. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The exhibit is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information is available at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Wellington Soccer Club sees record 840 registrations as World Cup excitement builds
cards.teaser: More than 840 children have registered to play with the Wellington Soccer Club for the upcoming season, a record turnout that coaches attribute to growing World Cup excitement across South Florida.
cards.body:
More than 840 children have registered to play with the Wellington Soccer Club for the upcoming season, a record turnout that coaches and organizers attribute to growing World Cup excitement across South Florida. At Greenview Shores Park, boys and girls are training with their sights set on the sport's biggest stage. Nine-year-old Parker dreams of playing professionally like Argentinian soccer star Tadeo Allende, who now plays for Inter Miami. "I want to be like Allende when I grow up, he's my favorite player," Parker said.

Patrick Zoete, the club's director of coaching, has taught the sport for more than 25 years. He said soccer offers young players far more than athletic development. "Soccer provides not only exercise but also a way of life for the kids to be part of a team, camaraderie. Some of them remain friends for life," Zoete said. He noted the surge in interest follows a pattern that repeats every four years. "We wait four years for a World Cup. I mean, it's huge. We're fortunate that we have Messi here at Inter Miami. We can go watch the best player in the world," Zoete said. The Wellington Soccer Club is one of many organizations across the area experiencing the spike in registrations.

cards.headline: Lawsuit challenges Florida property tax ballot language as biased ahead of November vote
cards.teaser: A lawsuit filed Thursday in Leon County challenges the property tax amendment ballot language approved by Florida lawmakers for November, arguing it uses campaign-style phrases and overstates what the proposal would accomplish.
cards.body:
A lawsuit filed Thursday in Leon County challenges the ballot language for a property tax amendment Florida lawmakers approved for the November 2026 General Election. The complaint, filed by a voter advocacy group and two registered voters, argues the language is "biased" and "misleading," claiming lawmakers used campaign-style phrases including "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes," "protecting small businesses" and "ensuring fairness." Attorney Jamie Cole, representing the plaintiffs, said ballot amendments should be neutral and accurate. "A ballot amendment is supposed to be fair, neutral, and not biased, and it's supposed to be accurate," Cole said. The lawsuit asks a judge to declare the wording unconstitutional and order Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite it within 10 days.

The lawsuit disputes several claims in the ballot summary. It challenges language suggesting the amendment guarantees funding for core services like police, firefighters, schools or infrastructure, and disputes claims that it protects small businesses when the amendment does not specifically mention them. The complaint also argues the summary overstates the proposal by suggesting it immediately exempts the first $250,000 of a home's value, when the initial exemption would be $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. On June 2, lawmakers passed legislation establishing this exemption schedule. The amendment requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters to become law.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium offers rare look at Florida coastal habitats
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce is inviting visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats with rare close-up encounters with marine life.
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to experience Florida's underwater world through live, working displays of coastal habitats. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the facility showcases marine life in settings that recreate actual ocean ecosystems rather than displaying animals in isolation. Manager Bill Hoffman explained that this approach to exhibiting fully functional ecosystem models has been the facility's cornerstone since 1980, distinguishing it from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV. The Fort Pierce location houses more species than many larger aquarium facilities across the country.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, a large display that brings one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems to life. Beyond the coral reef, visitors encounter live recreations of seagrass beds, mangrove habitats, and hardbottom communities. Each display demonstrates how different organisms depend on and interact with one another within their environment. Even smaller details capture attention, such as the facility's four-inch barracuda, which shows the diversity of marine life at different life stages.

A major draw for guests is the interactive touch tank, where visitors can handle marine species under the supervision of trained staff members. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran noted that guests will likely encounter animals they have never touched before. This hands-on experience allows people of all ages to develop a personal connection with marine life.

The exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station and focuses on educating the public about ocean conservation and environmental threats. Hoffman stressed that healthy ecosystems depend on numerous small organisms working together, a concept that the live displays help visitors understand. The facility remains open to the public year-round and plans upcoming programming tied to its 25th anniversary celebration later this year. For more information, visitors can check sms.si.edu and the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels. By bringing Florida's coastal habitats to visitors in their home region, the exhibit connects people to the importance and fragility of these marine environments.

cards.headline: Oxbridge Academy Thunderwolves see roster grow under new head coach Mike Colee
cards.teaser: The Oxbridge Academy Thunderwolves are back on the gridiron with new head football coach Mike Colee, who is already making an impact on roster numbers just weeks into his position.
cards.body:
Mike Colee, the newly named head football coach at Oxbridge Academy, is only a few weeks into his position but is already making an impact on the program's roster numbers. Colee said initial roster numbers were lower because everyone had made their summer plans before he was involved. Once he met with parents and kids and distributed the schedule, the numbers have been growing ever since.

As the season approaches, players said Colee's coaching style is already resonating with the team. Senior Cayden Pribramski said Colee is big on mental toughness and plays to the players' strengths. Pribramski noted that Colee is not the kind of guy to say "my way or the highway," but will build the program around players to help them succeed. The Thunderwolves are eager to put last year's 0-11 season behind them. Senior Brady Basis said the team wants to keep working and keep going, noting they came off a good spring win and want to bring that energy into the next season.

cards.headline: Wellington Soccer Club hits record 840 registrations as World Cup excitement sweeps South Florida
cards.teaser: More than 840 children have registered to play with the Wellington Soccer Club for the upcoming season, a record turnout that coaches and organizers attribute t.
cards.body:
More than 840 children have registered to play with the Wellington Soccer Club for the upcoming season, a record turnout that coaches and organizers attribute to growing World Cup excitement across South Florida. Patrick Zoete, the club's director of coaching, has taught the sport for more than 25 years and said soccer offers young players far more than athletic development. He noted that the surge in interest is a pattern that repeats every four years. "We're fortunate that we have Messi here at Inter Miami. We can go watch the best player in the world," Zoete said. The Wellington Soccer Club is one of many organizations across the area experiencing the spike.

At Greenview Shores Park, boys and girls are training with their sights set on the sport's biggest stage. Nine-year-old Parker wants to be like Tadeo Allende, the Argentinian soccer star who now plays for Inter Miami. Parker said he enjoys spending time with his friends, meeting new people every year, and feeling excited every time his team has a game. Zoete emphasized that soccer provides not only exercise but also a way of life for kids to be part of a team and build camaraderie. "Some of them remain friends for life," Zoete said.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses thrift stores to care for animals during Palm City shelter renovations
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to sustain animal care during a major renovation of its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily relocating many of its cats to the store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside unique items for sale at both thrift stores. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted. The organization is also seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. Donations of gently used goods are welcome at both locations. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Corpse flower nicknamed Princess Pungent could bloom within days at McKee Botanical Garden in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: A Titan Arum, also known as the corpse flower, is set to bloom at McKee Botanical Garden in Vero Beach and could open within the next few days or weeks.
cards.body:
The rare Titan Arum, also known as the corpse flower and nicknamed "Princess Pungent," is set to bloom within days or weeks at McKee Botanical Garden in Vero Beach, according to the garden's Instagram updates. The flower's bloom period typically lasts only 24 to 48 hours, during which it emits the stench of rotting flesh. The plant is native to the rainforests of Sumatra and Indonesia and is considered endangered.

This Titan Arum arrived at McKee in May 2026. In a Thursday update, the botanical garden reported the flower has grown nine inches taller, and one of its three remaining leaves has dropped, signaling that bloom time is approaching. McKee Botanical Garden's annual Waterlily Celebration takes place June 13, offering visitors the opportunity to witness and smell the full bloom.

cards.headline: Curaçao soccer fans travel from Port St. Lucie to Boca Raton training ahead of historic World Cup debut
cards.teaser: Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to witness Curaçao's Blue Wave prepare for their first-ever World Cup appearance this weekend, including fans who traveled from Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to witness Curaçao's preparation for its first-ever World Cup appearance. The team, known as the "Blue Wave," held a training session that drew enthusiastic supporters eager to see their favorite players ahead of the historic debut. Goalkeeper Eloy Room said the outpouring of support fueled the team's excitement. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today. It gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said. Curaçao, an island nation with a population of just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches.

Midfielder Tahitch Chong told WPTV the moment carries enormous meaning for both the players and the entire island. "I think it's amazing to see. I don't think the people back home are going to believe the crowd we had here," Chong said. Fans traveled from across South Florida, with some Curaçao natives making the drive from as far as Port St. Lucie. Marionella Barzeycoggins, originally from Curaçao, brought her whole family after learning about the training event. Local fan Bruce Zalman expressed enthusiasm about attending upcoming games at the Hard Rock. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas.

cards.headline: Lake Worth woman born without right hand goes viral after Palm Beach County deputy traffic stop
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Katie Thomas of Lake Worth for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, but Thomas was born without a right hand.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth resident Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas he observed her driving past him while holding and manipulating a phone with her right hand. Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. When the deputy pressed further, asking if she swore hand to God she did not have her phone in her hand, Thomas replied "Hand to God." The deputy then asked, "The other hand to God, you don't have a phone in your hand?" to which Thomas again replied "Hand to God."

Thomas was born without her right hand and has spent her life as an adaptive athlete raising awareness for the limb-difference community. She told WPTV that going viral was something she hoped would happen eventually, but not like this. "Literally being accused of something that I did not have a limb to be accused. I think that's probably one of the most captivating things about the whole thing, is that it was immediately apparent to 110 million people that what he claims he saw was impossible," Thomas said. The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. She said she has no plans to sue and hopes the attention helps people understand the limb difference community.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers rare look at Florida coastal ecosystems
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium welcomes visitors to discover Florida's coastal habitats through immersive encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. According to Manager Bill Hoffman, the facility has maintained its distinctive approach since 1980, focusing on fully live, complex ecosystem models that set it apart from typical public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said. The exhibit houses more species than many larger facilities, making it a unique destination for marine education.

The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef tank, which recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. The exhibit also features live representations of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each displaying the delicate relationships between organisms. Visitors can observe diverse marine life, including creatures as small as a four-inch barracuda. The touch tank remains one of the facility's most popular attractions, where guests can handle unusual marine species under the supervision of trained staff. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran noted that visitors often encounter animals they have never seen before. The facility is planning expanded programming for its 25th anniversary celebration later this year.

Operating in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit works to educate the public about ocean conservation and the threats facing marine environments. Hoffman stressed that healthy ecosystems depend on countless small organisms, a lesson reinforced through the facility's hands-on displays. By connecting visitors directly to Florida's marine life, the exhibit demonstrates why ocean health matters for the region and beyond.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and welcomes visitors year-round. For more information, visit sms.si.edu or follow the Smithsonian Marine Station on social media.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses Stuart thrift stores to shelter cats during Palm City facility renovations
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Shoppers can now find not only unique items for sale but also adoptable cats at both thrift stores. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said donations of gently used goods are welcome, noting that "every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals." The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library launches free summer STREAM programs for kids and teens
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library is offering kids and teens free STREAM programs in Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math, open to all Florida residents.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM programs — Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math — for kids and teens throughout the summer. Kae Jonsons, director of development and community relations, said the library has served the community since 1913, when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection. The library now welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually to its 36,000-square-foot facility at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue.

Young adult librarian Natalie Baron is leading sessions like ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also join lab-based activities, including collaborative 3D puzzle builds, and pick up themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, which encourages readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and take home an Unearth a Story bag with a free STREAM book and activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to youth up to 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children 5 and older to explore STREAM topics together. Upcoming Thursday guests include Malachi Fenn from the Florida Public Archaeology Network on June 11, Sea Turtle Adventures beach cleanup on June 25, American Shark Conservancy's SharkSmarts on July 2, and FPAN Beyond Artifacts on July 16. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: DeSantis criticizes Republican Party of Florida for canceling gubernatorial debate
hero.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis said Friday the Republican Party of Florida should not control debate criteria and criticized the party for canceling a planned debate at the upcoming Sunshine Showdown.
hero.body:
Ron DeSantis is challenging the Republican Party of Florida's decision to cancel a planned debate at the upcoming Sunshine Showdown event. DeSantis questioned why the party should be involved in structuring debates at all, arguing that candidates and media should drive the process instead.

DeSantis said the party announced it would hold a debate but never publicly released the qualifying criteria or held a vote to establish requirements. According to what he heard secondhand, the criteria included polling at 10% support in the party's own survey, raising more than $10 million, and securing more than 10,000 donors. DeSantis pointed out that he would not have met these standards when he ran for governor in 2018, arguing that trying to engineer outcomes through such requirements is counterproductive. Since Representative Byron Donalds meets the threshold, the party chose to allow candidates to speak individually rather than participate in a debate format, despite calls from Lieutenant Jay Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner for a traditional debate.

DeSantis emphasized that an open process where candidates can directly address voters is superior to attempting to predetermine results. He stressed that the party should prioritize what benefits Republican voters rather than pursuing its own agenda or answering to other interests. He called it ridiculous for the party to unilaterally set debate structures, noting that the party's role should be limited. DeSantis argued that debates should be candidate-driven affairs, not controlled by people whom voters have never elected to make such decisions. He suggested that candidates work directly with television stations, radio broadcasters, and other media outlets to arrange multiple opportunities for public appearances and debates.

DeSantis also noted the timing of his criticism, pointing out that qualifying closed at noon on Friday and many voters were not yet actively following the race. His comments highlight a broader debate within Republican circles about how primary elections should be structured and who should control the process of determining which candidates get significant media exposure before voters cast their ballots.

cards.headline: DeSantis grants Florida state workers five-day weekend for America 250 celebration
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Friday that Florida's 100,000 state employees will receive two additional days off in July, closing state offices on Thursday, J.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Friday that Florida's 100,000 state employees will receive two additional days off in July to celebrate America 250. State offices will be closed on Thursday, July 2, 2026, and Monday, July 6, 2026, giving state workers an extended weekend surrounding the nation's 250th anniversary of independence. "America's 250th anniversary is a historic milestone and an opportunity to reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and enduring principles that established the United States as the freest and most prosperous nation in the world," DeSantis said. He added that he is pleased to provide state employees additional time to celebrate the country's founding, participate in America 250 events, and spend time with family and friends honoring the blessings of liberty that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.

Florida has prioritized the semiquincentennial celebration under DeSantis's leadership. The governor has pointed out that Florida was the 14th colony at various points and has framed the celebration as a way to remind Floridians of American history and the state's unique role from the beginning of the Republic. As part of the celebration, DeSantis has focused on procuring statues of historic figures to display throughout the state, though not all of them are American presidents. He has also frequently cited Benjamin Franklin's memorable statement after the Constitution's ratification that the fledgling country was a Republic, if you can keep it.

cards.headline: Maxwell Frost secures third congressional term without named opponent in Orlando district
cards.teaser: Representative Maxwell Frost effectively won a third term in Congress Friday after qualifying showed his only opposition would come from a write-in candidate, making him the only member of Florida's congressional delegation to win the 2026 midterms without facing a named primary or general election opponent.
cards.body:
Maxwell Frost effectively won a third congressional term Friday after qualifying showed his only opposition would come from a write-in candidate. His write-in opponent, Brent Lawhon, has opened a federal campaign account, but his name will not appear on the ballot. Frost, an Orlando Democrat, thanked voters for the chance to serve and said the people of Central Florida continue to put their trust in him. He said his campaign has already brought on 87 campaign fellows this summer to help flip seats across Central Florida, defend Democratic champions, and make sure neighbors know their government is working for them.

Frost first won his seat in 2022, defeating a sitting state senator and two former members of Congress in the Democratic primary. He succeeded former U.S. Representative Val Demings, who stepped down to run for U.S. Senate. Frost won the general election that November with 59% of the vote. At age 25, he became the first Gen Z member of the U.S. House. Now 29 years old, Frost has developed a national profile as a progressive voice frequently featured on cable news. Florida's 10th Congressional District remains a safe blue seat, with more than 61% of voters supporting Democrat Kamala Harris for President in 2024.

cards.headline: 12 candidates file for Florida's 2nd Congressional District race to replace retiring Neal Dunn
cards.teaser: A dozen candidates qualified Friday for the race to replace retiring Representative Neal Dunn in Florida's 2nd Congressional District, including several prominent Republicans and four Democrats hoping to flip the Panhandle seat.
cards.body:
A crowded 12-person field qualified for Florida's 2nd Congressional District race to replace retiring Rep. Neal Dunn. The Republican field drew most candidates and fundraising attention. Keith Gross, an attorney who previously challenged Sen. Rick Scott in a GOP primary last year, leads as the top fundraiser. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power, a longtime Leon County GOP leader, also qualified for the ballot, along with Austin Rogers, a former staff counsel to Scott. Additional Republican candidates include Desert Storm pilot Lee Jon Jones, Kingdom Insurance owner Nick Lewis, Purple Heart veteran Luke Murphy, Gulf Coast Superintendent Jim Norton, and retired Leon Sheriff's Chief Deputy Audie Rowell.

Four Democrats qualified for the race. Attorney Yen Bailey, former foreign aid contractor Amanda Marie Green, and tech entrepreneur Nic Zateslo were already preparing to challenge Dunn when disabled families advocate Brice Barnes quickly entered the race following Dunn's departure announcement. The district voted for Donald Trump with 59 percent in 2024 compared to 40 percent for Democrat Kamala Harris. However, Dunn succeeded Democratic former Rep. Gwen Graham, who was tapped as gubernatorial candidate David Jolly's running mate, giving Democrats hope for a potential Panhandle seat flip. The district covers much of the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, stretching from Defuniak Springs in the west to Perry and Madison in the east, including Tallahassee and Panama City.

cards.headline: Former Representative Jackie Toledo challenges Harry Cohen for Hillsborough County Commission as Susan Valds withdraws
cards.teaser: Former Representative Jackie Toledo filed Friday to challenge incumbent Commissioner Harry Cohen for Hillsborough County Commission District 1, while Susan Valds ended her short-lived bid for District 5.
cards.body:
Susan Valdés is withdrawing from her bid for Hillsborough County Commission District 5 after filing last week, citing family health reasons. Valdés posted on social media Thursday that a personal family health matter requires her full focus, time, and presence. She had entered a Republican primary that already included incumbent Commissioner Donna Cameron Cepeda and Hillsborough County School Board Member Stacy Hahn. Democrat Neil Manimala is also running for the countywide seat. Rumors circulated this week that Valdés was contemplating switching to the District 1 race, but the Hillsborough County Supervisor of Elections confirmed she did not redesignate to another district.

Former Rep. Jackie Toledo filed Friday to run in District 1, challenging incumbent Commissioner Harry Cohen in his re-election bid. Toledo, a Tampa Republican and former House District 60 lawmaker, previously ran for Congress in Florida's 15th Congressional District after leaving the House. She was known during her time in Tallahassee for work on human trafficking legislation and Pharmacy Benefit Manager oversight. Cohen, a Democrat and former Tampa City Council member, first won the District 1 seat in 2020. The Hillsborough County Supervisor of Elections lists both Cohen and Toledo as qualified. Valdés indicated she may still run for office at another time or continue serving the community as a public servant in some other capacity.

cards.headline: Growth debate dominates St. Johns County Commission races as qualifying closes
cards.teaser: Growth and development remain central issues in St. Johns County's 2026 elections as candidate qualifying closed Friday, finalizing races that will gauge voter sentiment in one of Florida's fastest-growing counties.
cards.body:
District 2 Commissioner Sarah Arnold is not seeking re-election, resulting in an open seat with four Republican candidates. Former FBI agent Martin Pysczymuka is campaigning under the slogan "Slow the growth, stop the waste." William McMullan emphasizes balancing economic development with preservation, advocating for "smarter planning" and supporting manufacturing and aerospace job growth. Johns County Sheriff's Captain Tim Burres cites overdevelopment as a primary campaign issue. Citibank executive Heather Brofford entered the race shortly before the qualifying deadline, with priorities including transportation improvements, public safety, emergency services, and infrastructure investments. As of the end of May, Pysczymuka leads fundraising with nearly $28,000, closely followed by McMullan with approximately $27,000.

In District 4, first-term Commissioner Krista Joseph faces two Republican challengers. Joseph was elected in 2022 after defeating incumbent Commissioner Jeremiah Blocker in the Republican Primary, despite being significantly outspent. Since taking office, she has consistently opposed rapid growth but has also generated controversy. In December 2023, fellow Commissioners formally censured her after she urged voters from the dais to remove her colleagues from office. Joseph later filed a lawsuit against the other four Commissioners but ultimately dropped the case. Retired law enforcement officer Samuel Williams leads fundraising in the race with more than $56,000 raised, more than double Joseph's total. Attorney James Galloway also qualified for the ballot, citing congestion and rapid growth as the county's most pressing concerns. Both contests will be decided in the August primary under Florida law allowing all registered voters to participate.

cards.headline: 11 Broward and Palm Beach County incumbents win unopposed as qualifying ends
cards.teaser: Several incumbents in Broward and Palm Beach counties will return to office without facing voters after being the only candidates to qualify in their respective races by the noon deadline Friday.
cards.body:
Several incumbents in Broward and Palm Beach counties will return to office without facing voters after qualifying closed Friday at noon. Three Broward County Commission incumbents, Mayor Mark Bogen in District 2, Vice Mayor Robert McKinzie in District 8, and Lamar Fisher in District 4, all Democrats, secured re-election without opposition. Four county judges also drew no challengers: Ellen Feld, Allison Gilman, Phoebee Francois, and Michele Ricca. In Palm Beach County, School Board District 3 incumbent Karen Brill was similarly returned to office without a contest. County Judges Santo DiGangi, M. Katherine Mullinax, and Reginald Corlew also ran unopposed.

Voters will weigh in on 13 other County Commission and School Board races across the two counties. While County Commission contests in Broward and Palm Beach are partisan, School District races are technically nonpartisan, meaning all qualified candidates will appear on the August ballot. A candidate must receive more than 50% of the vote in the primary to win outright. If no candidate does, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. The only contested Commission race in Broward is in District 6, where four Democrats are vying to succeed outgoing Commissioner Beam Furr. Hollywood Commissioner Caryl Shuham, former Broward Director of Policy and Public Affairs Eugen Bold, former Dania Beach Mayor Archibald Ryan, and maritime business owner Jeffrey Jones, who unsuccessfully challenged Furr in 2022, all qualified for the race.

hero.headline: Debate continues over Brightline station proposal in Stuart
hero.body:
Stuart city officials continue to debate whether to pursue a Brightline passenger rail station within city limits. The discussion centers on how the city would accommodate a station for the high-speed rail service that currently operates between Miami and Orlando.

The debate reflects ongoing conversations about transportation infrastructure in Stuart. City leaders are weighing the potential benefits of improved rail connectivity against concerns about implementation and location.

Brightline trains currently pass through Martin County on tracks owned by Florida East Coast Railway. The railroad corridor runs through downtown Stuart, making station placement a key consideration in any discussions.

City officials have not announced a timeline for making a decision on the station proposal. The ongoing debate comes as Brightline continues to expand its service throughout Florida.

cards.headline: Fantini's Fusion Kitchen opens today in Palm City
cards.teaser: A new restaurant opened its doors in Palm City on Friday.
cards.body:
Fantini's Fusion Kitchen opened June 12 in Palm City. The restaurant marks a new dining option for residents in the Martin County community.

The opening adds to the commercial landscape in Palm City. The restaurant's opening comes as the area continues to see business development along its main corridors.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide in Fort Pierce shooting
cards.teaser: A teenager faces an attempted homicide charge after a Thursday night shooting left another 16-year-old in critical condition in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old faces an attempted homicide charge following a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. Detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and observed three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Officers discovered another juvenile lying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. The 16-year-old victim was in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One suspect was caught by a sheriff's office K9, while another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence, and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with killing grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: A 29-year-old Vero Beach man is accused of killing his 76-year-old grandmother, who was found dead inside her home in February.
cards.body:
A 29-year-old Vero Beach man now faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of his 76-year-old grandmother. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that Nicholas Leonard Ivey is accused of killing Patricia Ann DiBella, who had opened her home to him at her residence at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. According to investigators, Ivey admitted to killing DiBella on Feb. 1. The following day, family members requested a welfare check that led deputies to the scene, where Ivey was taken into custody. Ivey has been held on other related charges since February and was formally charged with murder on June 3.

Ivey is being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond. Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement that no one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. The sheriff's office reminded the community that domestic violence can take many forms and affect anyone. Those in danger are encouraged to call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023 or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

cards.headline: Driver charged with vehicular homicide 8 months after I-95 crash in Boynton Beach killed 92-year-old woman
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County man faces a vehicle homicide charge eight months after a crash on Interstate 95 in Boynton Beach killed a woman three days before her 93rd birthday.
cards.body:
Guy Augustin, 22 at the time of the collision, was arrested Wednesday and booked at the Palm Beach County jail on a vehicular homicide charge eight months after the Oct. 8, 2025 crash. The two-vehicle wreck occurred at about 9:45 p.m. on southbound I-95 just south of the Gateway Boulevard exit in Boynton Beach, killing Martha Gutierrez, who was three days away from her 93rd birthday. According to a probable cause affidavit, Augustin was driving a 2013 BMW 535i when he changed lanes improperly, moving behind Gutierrez's Toyota Camry and hitting her vehicle in the rear. The impact sent Gutierrez's car into a concrete barrier wall and Augustin's BMW off the road and into the grass.

Gutierrez was taken to Delray Medical Center but was pronounced dead at 11:22 p.m. Investigators said Augustin admitted to traveling at speeds of 95-100 mph in a 65 mph speed zone and following two motorcycles too closely before the collision. A witness reported that Augustin passed her at a high rate of speed while weaving in and out of traffic at about 80 mph. FHP data from the BMW showed speeds of 123 mph, then 119 mph until impact at 117 mph. Event Data Recorder data indicated the impact speed was between 111.24 and 132.41 mph. Augustin, who lives near West Palm Beach, is being held on a $100,000 bond.

cards.headline: DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud prevention measures at West Palm Beach press conference
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis announced sweeping new Medicaid fraud prevention measures during a press conference Friday afternoon in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis announced sweeping new Medicaid fraud prevention measures during a press conference Friday in West Palm Beach at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County. DeSantis said the state is partnering with President Donald Trump's administration and federal agencies to combat Medicaid fraud, identifying southeast Florida as particularly concentrated with fraud hotspots. Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. Harris described how investigators discovered the fake operations through shared addresses across multiple unrelated entities, suspicious ownership structures, and no evidence of actual patient care.

The state announced three major initiatives to address fraud. AHCA is launching a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company that will identify stolen IDs, synthetic IDs, and hidden ownership structures. AHCA has imposed enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories, including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers. The state is launching a comprehensive revalidation effort requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to verify their credentials and identity. Harris said Florida's program integrity efforts have already saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits. Over the past two years, AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers. Florida's Medicaid program covers nearly 4 million recipients statewide.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County deputy accuses Lake Worth woman of holding phone with hand she doesn't have in viral traffic stop
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over a Lake Worth woman for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. She was born without a right hand.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Katie Thomas of Lake Worth for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. The traffic stop went viral on social media, generating 110 million views. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas he observed her "holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. Thomas was born without her right hand and has spent her life as an adaptive athlete, raising awareness for the limb-difference community. She told reporters that going viral was something she had hoped would happen eventually, but not under these circumstances. "Literally being accused of something that I did not have a limb to be accused. I think that's what's probably one of the most captivating things about the whole thing, is that it was immediate, immediately apparent to 110 million people, that what he claims he saw was impossible," Thomas said.

The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas said she harbors no ill will against the sheriff's office and would be open to a conversation about using the moment to spread awareness about the limb difference community. She has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. Thomas said she has no plans to sue and hopes the attention helps people better understand the limb difference community.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium showcases Florida coastal habitats
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce offers visitors close encounters with marine life through fully live ecosystem models dating back to 1980.
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's vibrant underwater world through live, complex ecosystem displays. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce's waterfront district, the facility has maintained a unique philosophy since 1980 by showcasing fully functioning marine habitats rather than static displays. Manager Bill Hoffman told WPTV that the approach sets the aquarium apart from most public facilities. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said. Despite its modest size, the facility houses more species than many larger aquariums across the country.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, a sprawling display that recreates one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems in vivid detail. Beyond the coral reef, visitors encounter live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. Each habitat demonstrates the intricate relationships between organisms that make these ecosystems thrive. Even smaller creatures play critical roles, such as the facility's four-inch barracuda, which contributes to the complex food webs on display.

The touch tank has become a visitor favorite, offering hands-on experiences with marine species under staff supervision. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran notes that guests often encounter animals they have never seen before while handling creatures from the live displays. This interactive component helps visitors develop a deeper connection to the marine life they learn about throughout the exhibit. The facility plans to expand its programming offerings later this year as part of its 25th anniversary celebration.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates through a partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station and focuses on educating the public about ocean conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable marine ecosystems depend on countless small organisms working together, a lesson reinforced by the facility's live displays. With growing concerns about ocean health, exhibits like this one provide valuable educational opportunities for visitors of all ages to understand the fragile beauty and ecological importance of Florida's marine environments. The facility is open to the public year-round, and more information is available at sms.si.edu and through the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after Fort Pierce shooting leaves teen in critical condition
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old faces an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce left another teen in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects, with one caught by a sheriff's office K9 and another found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene.

The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murder of 76-year-old grandmother who welcomed him into her home
hero.body:
A 29-year-old Vero Beach man has been formally charged with murdering his 76-year-old grandmother, who was discovered dead in her home in February. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the charges against Nicholas Leonard Ivey on Friday. He faces both murder and tampering with physical evidence charges in connection with the death of Patricia Ann DiBella. According to investigators, Ivey admitted to killing his grandmother, who had allowed him to live at her residence located at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach.

The discovery of DiBella's body came after family members requested a welfare check the day following her death. When deputies arrived at the home, they found Ivey present and took him into custody at that time. Though arrested in February, Ivey remained in custody on other related charges until the sheriff's office formally charged him with murder on June 3. He continues to be held at the Indian River County Jail without the possibility of bond.

In a statement regarding the case, Sheriff Eric Flowers expressed his approval of the investigative work completed by his team. "I am proud of the work our investigations team did to bring justice to Patricia DiBella and her family. No one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. I encourage anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement," Flowers said. The sheriff's office used the case as an opportunity to remind the community that domestic violence can manifest in different ways and impact people across all backgrounds and circumstances.

Individuals who believe they or someone they know is in danger are urged to take action. The sheriff's office encourages residents to call 911 in emergency situations. Additional resources available to those experiencing domestic violence include SafeSpace, which can be reached at 772-288-7023, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. These services provide support and guidance for those dealing with domestic violence situations.
